content.text:
I like it, with one change: make the feed its own content type instead of building it out of your existing reflections.

Right now `reflections` uses the garden schema. Each one has a title, a status (seedling → evergreen) and an `updatedAt`, so they're notes you keep coming back to and growing. A Twitter/Instagram-style post works the other way. It has a timestamp, often no title, and once it's posted it stays as it was. Forcing feed posts into the garden model would muddy both.

Here's how I'd set it up:

- **A new `feed` collection** with one small file per post. The only required field is `date`. Text (the body) and `images` are both optional. A text-only post is a tweet; a post with images is an Instagram post, and both appear in one stream.
- **Feed posts can also point to garden content.** When you publish or update a reflection, a feed post can link to it, like sharing your own blog post on social media. The garden stays the place for deeper work, and the feed is the timeline.
- **Possibly fold `photos`/`albums` in.** An album could just be a feed post with several images, which would mean one less concept to maintain.

The appeal of this approach is that you own it, it's plain markdown in git, and a Danish visitor gets a real sense of who you are and what you're doing. That fits the "show real work" goal better than polished pages alone.

Some questions before building anything:

1. Should reflections become feed posts, or should the feed only link to them?
2. Do you want albums/photos merged into the feed, or kept as a separate gallery?
3. Should each post have its own page (`/feed/2026-10-25-...`) that you can share, or does the stream alone work for you?
4. Where should the feed live: the homepage, or `/feed` linked from it?

Yes, we remove reflections and albums. Everything is on feed instead. We should show it as a scroll feed. Where when we click on each, it takes us to its own page.

content.text:
The feed is live at `/feed`, and reflections, albums and the photos page are gone. The production build passes. I haven't viewed it in a browser since you're starting the server yourself, so run `npx astro dev` and open `/feed`.

**How it works**
- All posts now live in one folder, `src/content/feed/`, one markdown file per post. The only required field is `date`; `title` is optional.
- `/feed` lists everything newest first:
  - **Posts with photos** show as albums: just the title, the date and the photos in your swipeable carousel.
  - **Posts without photos** show the title, then the text cut to about 280 characters with a "Keep reading →" link. A short post fits in full, like a tweet.
- Clicking any post opens its own page at `/feed/<filename>`, with a "Feed · date" line above the full post.

**What moved**
- `copenhagen-2024.md` and `to-write-again.md` moved into `src/content/feed/`. The reflection lost its `status`/`updatedAt` fields and `createdAt` became `date`.
- I deleted the `/reflections`, `/albums` and `/photos` pages. Old links (including the two old post URLs) now redirect to the feed.
- The Garden now covers only essays and explorations.
- The new post layout for text is in `src/components/TextPost.astro`, the feed logic is in `src/lib/feed.ts`, and the album carousel still uses `AlbumPost.astro`.

**Things to know**
- **No Feed link in the menu yet.** Your header links were already commented out, so I swapped the old Photos/Albums links there for a Feed link, still commented out. Uncomment it in `src/layouts/Layout.astro` when you want it visible.
- **Feed previews are plain text.** Links and bold/italic show as ordinary text in the cut-down version on `/feed`; the post's own page keeps all formatting.
- **New post:** to add one, create a file like `src/content/feed/my-post.md`. Text only makes a text post; add a photo the same way as in your Copenhagen album (with `?width=&height=` in the URL) and it becomes an album.

---
title: "I want to write again"
date: 2026-08-19
---
I have been struggling to write down this piece for quite a while. I think I have been trying to define the perfect structure for my website so finally, when it is done, I can publish my thoughts. I think I was just delaying the process of writing again.

I feel that the last time I wrote something, I was focusing too much into making something useful for the world. I felt as if whatever I published, was going to be the next piece I was going to be proud of. However, a question kept crawling my mind: What is it worth?

Ever since I can recall, I have been in love with writing. Not necessarily essays, but also poems, thoughts, and other forms of expressing our minds. I adore to understand new languages and learn about all the possible ways they are connected. There is just so much, we as species, have develop in order to work together.

With AI taking over everything that means knowledge work, I have lost the spark I felt when I thought of writing. It felt as if every piece of text was just a regurgitated blob of statistically generated strings that somehow made sense. It felt as we started to devalue our own communication, and start optimising towards the machines. Of course, this is not only a tech issue. It is a social issue. It is linked to fascism, capitalism, patriarchy and multiple other fields of knowledge coming from social sciences.

Every entry on `/feed` now uses the same layout: the date in small text, then the title as a heading, then the content. The only difference is that content:

- **Posts with photos** show the carousel.
- **Posts without photos** show the shortened text and a "Keep reading →" link when it's cut off.

The date, the title and the photos all link to the post's own page. The type check reports no errors and the build passes, but I haven't looked at the page in a browser.

In the code, both kinds of post now go through one component, `src/components/FeedPost.astro`. `AlbumPost.astro` became `Carousel.astro` and now contains only the carousel, and `TextPost.astro` is gone.

This means albums now show the title as a full heading, like text posts, instead of the small "title · date" line they had before. If you'd rather everything use the small style, that's a one-line change.

Not sure if I want to date exactly the photo albums. Maybe in the future I will want a text only feed entry to not be dated, just month shuld be enough. Should we do a way to do that? That with a flag or setting the day as 00 of the date that we only show in the month, so it goes to the top of the month entries or so?

Yes, I'd add it, but a day of `00` won't work. It isn't a valid date, so the build would reject it, or JavaScript would quietly turn it into the last day of the previous month. A separate flag field is extra to remember. I'd rather let `date` take just the year and month:

```yaml
date: 2024-11      # shows "November 2024"
date: 2024-11-17   # shows "17.11.2024", as now
```

As you suggested, month-only posts will sit at the top of their month. I'm implementing that now.

## Weekly realizations

**I love remote work** - I saw some threads on Twitter about how people would even ask for a 100% increase on their salaries to convince them to go back to an office job. ## Weekly realizations

**HTML is simple but not easy** - This week I had some talks with friends about how creating websites and using HTML is something considered easy. However, I believe that that is true if you don't consider accessibility as part of creating good HTML markup. When the HTML code we write is not semantic, we are making it hard, not only for computers but also humans, to have a good experience in our websites. Being able to navigate a website with the keyboard should make things easier for the user and would bring many benefits even for SEO.

**Time blocking calendars should be updated from time to time** - I am a believer in time blocking. It is a productivity method to group tasks of one type in a time slot so there are fewer switches of context. This week I noticed that my usual calendar was not working well because it was created almost a year ago. And my reality is much more different from what it was then. So this is your reminder to update your time blocking calendars.

This week I started a new initiative called #historiasquenovemos. It is a small organization to allow men to show their emotions, break gender stereotypes and work against the privileges that were given to men just because of our gender. We are planning to share useful information, personal stories, and book recommendations in our website. You can know more about the project in our website:

The Workbench is up at `/workbench`, and "explorations" is now **notes** in your Garden. The type check is clean and the build passes, but I haven't looked at either page in a browser.

**Workbench**
- All 10 projects from your old `works` folder are copied into `src/content/workbench/`. Your originals in `personal-website` are untouched.
- They're listed newest first and grouped by year. Each one shows its title, description, and "type · role · with …".
- Only projects with real write-ups get their own page: **YLMA**, **Buy a Brick** and **Un-fair**. The other seven show as a plain line with no link, so nobody clicks through to an empty page.
- A YouTube link or an `.mp4` link on its own line now becomes an embedded video. YouTube uses the privacy-friendly no-cookie player, and your ImageKit videos get a preview frame. The plugin is `src/lib/rehype-videos.ts`. Buy a Brick has all 6 of its videos, and YLMA has its trailer, two clips and the editing screenshot.
- Each project now has only `title`, `date`, `description`, `type`, `role` and optionally `with`.

**Garden**
- Following Maggie Appleton: essays are opinionated long-form writing with an agenda, and notes are loose notes on things you don't fully understand yet. Both keep the seedling/budding/evergreen stages.
- `/notes` replaces `/explorations`, with her description of notes as the subtitle.

**Things I left out or noticed**
- **Placeholder text dropped:** HQNV, OPENschool, Empoderando Juventudes, Letting Go, Quantic Games and Raaz all had the same placeholder text in your old files: "Co-founder, Technical lead" plus the same YouTube link. I didn't copy that text over. Raaz's video is the placeholder one too, so I think its real link is missing. Send it and Raaz can get its own page.
- **Categories dropped:** every old project had the category "Video Production", including the startups and the book, so I didn't carry it over.
- **Notes is empty:** the Notes section still has no live posts. Your three notes and two essay drafts are files without a `.md` extension, so the site skips them. I've assumed they're drafts and left them. That's also why the build warns that "notes" is empty.
- **Essay date typo:** "A blurry past" has `updatedAt: 2-07-11`, which looks like a typo for 2021-07-11. Its description, about hosting your own writing, also seems to belong to a different piece. I haven't changed either.

The Workbench isn't linked from the menu or homepage yet. Since you want the site to show off your work, I'd add a Workbench section to the homepage next to the Garden. Should I?

OK, not sure if the way of showing the metadata of the projects on the list is fine. What would make it better? Like, in a way that is clean but also informative and showcase that I am a diverse person by nature

Right now every row gives type, role and partner equal weight in one grey line, so the most interesting fact gets lost. That fact is that the list mixes a startup, a music video, a book and a comic. I'd make the **type** the visible signal and put everything else behind it.

The type and role line already says *what* it is ("Music video · Director, Cinematographer & Editor"), so the one-liner doesn't need to repeat that. It should give the hook: the detail that makes someone click. Aim for one sentence that fits on at most two lines, about 100–140 characters.

3. *"A circular story about the macho influencer persona. Vishay Khxl plays both roles, shot in Copenhagen with no crew and no split screen."*

I'd go with **1** or **2**. They keep your original idea but add the twist (one artist playing two roles), which makes people curious. Option 3 is the most impressive about your craft, but production details like "no crew" land better on the project page itself.

Listing every job title makes the line long and reads a bit like a CV. Some shorter options:

1. **"Director"**: in music videos, the director usually also writes the concept, so this one word covers most of what you did. It's the most standard credit. Your project page already has a Credits section, so the camera and editing work still gets mentioned there.
2. **"Writer, director & editor"**: still a list of titles, but in the usual film-credit order and a bit shorter. "Director" covers recording well enough; in small productions directors often shoot their own work.
3. **"Wrote, shot & edited"**: verbs instead of titles. This is the most honest and human version: it says exactly what you did, in plain words, which fits how you write. It also makes clear you did it all yourself. The other projects use titles ("Video producer", "Co-author"), so this one would stand out a little. That might be fine, since it's your biggest solo piece.

I don't think so. The whole site sits in a narrow left-hand column (`max-w-xl`, with the header pinned top-left). If only the project pages were centred, they would look like they belong to a different site, and the text would sit away from your name and the nav.

Photos already do a mild version of this with the `bleed` class, so it would just go further on project pages.

Should we add the dots in triangle svg for the projects or for the feed entries?

No, I wouldn't. The three dots work on the homepage because they're rare: two entries saying "start here." Repeated beside every project and feed post, they become decoration, the lists get busier, and the mark stops meaning anything. Both lists are already easy to scan because the titles do that work.

I'd keep the dots as a small signature for places that point somewhere, like the homepage list, or a "where to go next" link at the end of a project or post if you add one later. That keeps them special and still ties the pages together.
Not sure how to make the feed more special?

I think the feed's problem is the content more than the design. Right now every entry is a titled reflection of a few hundred words, plus one album, so it reads like a blog archive. Twitter and Instagram feel alive because the posts come in different shapes. Some ideas:

1. **Short posts shown in full.** A post with no title and a few sentences would appear whole, not truncated and not a link, like a tweet. A thought, a quote, a song you're listening to. The schema already allows posts without titles, so this is a small change.
2. **Single photos.** One picture with a line under it, shown large, not as a carousel album. This is the Instagram half of the idea, and it's quick to post.
3. **A personal touch with your handwriting font.** The site already loads Reenie Beanie for your name. A small handwritten note on some posts, like a place ("Copenhagen") or a mood, would feel like *you* in a way no other list on the site does. Used sparingly, it would make the feed the warm corner of the site.

I'd start with 1 and 3. Short posts give you a reason to post often, and that's what makes a feed feel like a feed. The handwritten notes give it character without adding clutter.

content.text:
I read through it. Smidgeons shows every entry in full, with no truncation, and that only works because the entries are tiny: a few sentences, a link, sometimes an image. Her longer writing lives in Essays and Notes, not in the stream. A few things you could take from it:

1. **A one-line intro under the heading.** Hers says roughly "a stream of interesting links, papers, and tiny thoughts." Your feed has no description right now, so visitors don't know what it is. This is the easiest win. It should be in your words, something along the lines of "Photos and short thoughts, as they happen," but you'd phrase it better.
2. **Link posts.** Many of her entries are a link to something she read, with the title pointing to the source and a few lines of her own thoughts below. That fits next to your tweets if you ever share articles or videos. It would be a small schema addition: an optional `url`, so the title links out with the arrow, like the external projects on the workbench.
3. **Tiny posts don't need their own page.** Hers link to an anchor on the stream itself. Your short posts already have the date as a permalink, so this is optional.

It also answers the truncation question. Her stream feels good because short things show in full and long things live elsewhere. Your long reflections are the only entries that need truncating. If you keep them in the feed, 4–6 lines is right. If you see them more as writing than as posts, they could become notes in the Garden, and the feed would be purely photos and tweets with nothing truncated. That's the bigger decision.

Where do you see the reflections living: in the feed, or in the Garden?
Where should they live?

I'd keep them in the feed.

By your own definitions, the Garden holds things you keep tending, evergreen notes and essays that grow over time. The reflections aren't like that. Each one captures what you were living through in a particular week. They're dated, personal, and finished when posted; you won't go back and update "It takes time to heal". That's what a feed post is: a moment in time. They're just longer than a tweet.

In the Garden they'd also be out of place. The Garden shows when a note was last tended and how far along it is, from seedling to evergreen, and neither means anything for a reflection from 2021.

So the feed holds three kinds of post: photos, tweets, and the occasional longer reflection, which is the one kind that gets truncated. That's normal for a personal stream. Instagram has long captions and Twitter has threads.

The one exception: if a reflection ever turns into something you keep rethinking and adding to, that's the time to rewrite it as a Garden note. You'd promote it on purpose rather than move all of them.
What if in the feed we just expand within the page, never we make it into new pages? Even the albums?

I think it's a good idea, with one condition: keep the individual pages quietly in the background and stop linking to them from the feed.

**What gets better:**
- The feed feels like a real stream. You read, expand and keep scrolling, without page loads or back buttons.
- Albums fit well. The carousel already holds every photo, so expanding would only reveal the album's text and captions underneath.
- It's closer to Smidgeons, Twitter and Instagram, where you rarely leave the stream.

**What you'd lose if the pages disappeared entirely:**
- **Sharing a single post.** You couldn't send someone "Copenhagen" on its own. When a link is shared in a chat or on social media, the preview image and title come from the post's own page.
- **Old links.** `/albums/copenhagen-2024` and `/reflections/to-write-again` currently redirect to those pages.
- **Page weight.** The full text of every reflection would load into `/feed`. That's fine with ten posts, less fine with a hundred.

So: posts expand in place on the feed, and the date stays a small permalink to the post's own page, like the short posts have now. Nobody needs the pages while scrolling, but they're there when you share something.

To expand, you'd click the truncated text and it opens to the full post right there, with no button taking up space. A small "Show less" at the bottom would collapse it again.

Damn, so good. Now the feed looks special.

How can we make the workbench to look special now?

Now that the feed has a personality, the workbench can get its own in a different way. What makes it unique is that most of your projects are visual (music videos, a comic, video campaigns), yet the list is text only. Ideas, roughly from most to least impact:

1. **Hover previews.** On desktop, hovering a project shows a small image of it floating beside the cursor: a still from YLMA, a Letting Go panel, a frame from Buy a Brick. Many designer portfolios do this, and it fits your lean style because nothing changes until you hover. The list stays clean, but it suddenly shows the work. On phones nothing changes. YouTube projects already have thumbnails we can use, and for the others you'd pick an image.
2. **Handwritten notes, borrowed from the feed.** An optional `note` per project, like "my first music video" or "still proud of this one", in the same hand beside the year. It connects the two pages and adds the honest, personal voice that portfolios usually lack. Use it on two or three projects, not all.
3. **Filter by type.** A row of small words at the top, like "All · Music videos · Organizations · Startups · Books · Comics". Clicking one filters the list. It makes the "I'm diverse by nature" point at a glance, before anyone reads a single entry. With only 10 projects it's less necessary, but it would grow with you.

I'd do 1 and 2. The previews make it feel like a portfolio of real work, which matters for the Denmark audience you mentioned. The notes make it feel like yours.

For the hover previews: do you have images in mind for the projects without videos, like Difficult Hugs, HQNV and the startups? Or should those just have no preview?
Maybe we add images for each? Give me other ideas?

Yes, images for every project is the right base. They make hover previews possible, and they're useful later for the detail pages and for link previews when someone shares a project. It would be one optional `image` field per project. For the videos I can pull the YouTube thumbnails, and for the rest you'd choose a photo: the Difficult Hugs cover, an HQNV event, a startup screenshot or logo.

Other ideas beyond the first three:

4. **A featured project at the top.** Your strongest or most recent piece (probably YLMA) shown bigger, with its image. Everything else stays in the lean list below. It's how most portfolios lead: one thing done well before the full list.
5. **"Currently working on."** A small line or pinned entry at the top for what's on your bench right now, even unfinished. It suits the workbench name and tells visitors you're active, not just showing an archive.
6. **Status, like the Garden.** A tiny marker for whether a project is ongoing or finished ("still running", "wrapped up in 2023"). It's honest, and it shows that organizations like HQNV are part of a longer story.
7. **Always-visible thumbnails.** A small square image to the left of each entry, all the time, not just on hover. Easier to scan and works on phones, but it makes the page busier than your current style.
8. **A grid view.** The projects as an image grid, like an Instagram profile, with a toggle between grid and list. It's striking, but it's a bigger departure, and the descriptions get hidden.

My pick is **images for all + hover previews (1) + a featured project (4)**. The featured project gives a strong first impression, and the hover previews make the rest of the list come alive without cluttering it. Notes (2) and "currently working on" (5) are small personal touches you can add any time.

Which of these appeal to you? Once you've picked, I'll set up the `image` field and pull the YouTube thumbnails so you only need to add images for the non-video projects.

Here are three ways to use handwriting, images, or both, each with an example of how it would look.

**A. Handwritten margin notes**: handwriting only, no images needed.

```

macho-influencer alter ego...

2021 · Organization · Co-founder

A pro-feminist space for men in Latin America...

A few words in your handwriting beside two or three projects, like notes written in the margin of your own CV. It's the cheapest option and it fits the feed's notes.

**B. Polaroid on hover**: handwriting and images together.

```
You Love My Arrogance ◄ hover
Vishay Khxl plays both himself...      ┌─────────────┐
                                       │             │
                                       │   [still]   │
                                       │             │
                                       │  shot in 2  │  ← handwriting
                                       └─────────────┘     tilted ~3°
```

Hovering a project shows its image as a slightly tilted polaroid, with a short caption in your handwriting under the photo, like photos pinned up on a real workbench. On phones nothing changes.

**C. A scrapbook strip at the top**: images and handwriting, always visible.

```
Workbench

 ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐   ┌──────┐
 │ YLMA │ ┌──────┐ │  │      │
 │      │ │ comic│ │  │ book │

  ylma    └──────┘   diff. hugs

A consolidated list of all the things...
```

Three or four of your favourite projects as overlapping, tilted photos with handwritten labels, sitting above the intro. Clicking one goes to its project. It works on phones too, and it's the most striking first impression of the three.

I'd go with **B**. It's the most "you": personal, playful, and the list stays lean until you hover. A and B also work together, with margin notes on a few entries and polaroids on all of them.

I looked at portfolio index galleries, Framer's hover-list patterns and indie-web sites. Five ideas I hadn't suggested yet:

**1. Video on hover ("reel index").** Hovering a row opens it to play a muted clip of the project, while the other rows dim. Framer's ReelIndex and several designer portfolios do this. You already have short `.mp4` clips on ImageKit for YLMA, so the work literally moves.

```
2025 · Music video
You Love My Arrogance       ┌──────────────────┐
                            │ ▶ muted clip     │   ← other rows fade to 40%
                            └──────────────────┘
```

**2. A contact sheet with grease-pencil marks.** Photographers mark their favourite frames on a contact sheet with a red grease pencil. The page would open with a strip of small frames from your projects, with hand-drawn circles around a few and a handwritten word beside them. It's images and handwriting together, and it comes from a real photographers' tradition, which suits you.

```
┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐
│ ▢  │(▢) │ ▢  │ ▢  │(▢) │ ▢  │   ← circled in orange, hand-drawn
└────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘
       ylma!            letting go

**3. Hand-drawn marks on the list.** A small library, Rough Notation (about 4kb), draws sketchy circles, underlines and brackets that animate in as you scroll. I searched elsewhere this time: brutalist and typographic portfolios, object-themed sites (shelves, desks) and tactile card designs. All of these work the same on mobile and desktop:

**8. A wall of names (typographic poster).** Inspired by type-led studios like Problem Studio. All project titles flow together as one big serif paragraph, like a poster. Tapping a name opens its details underneath. It's text only, very lean, and the variety of your work shows at a glance.

```
You Love My Arrogance / Raaz / Difficult Hugs /
Buy a Brick / Un-fair / Empoderando Juventudes /
#HQNV / Letting Go / OpenSchool / Quantic Games
```

**9. Stacked cards on scroll.** Inspired by Framer's "Scroll Stack Deck". Each project is a card, and as you scroll, each new card slides up over the previous one like a growing pile on a desk. It can be pure CSS (`position: sticky`) with no JavaScript, and it feels tactile on a phone.

**10. A bookshelf.** Inspired by Denisa Coteanu's "library" portfolio. Projects as book spines standing side by side, the title written vertically and tinted by type. Tapping one pulls it out and shows its details. It scrolls sideways on mobile. It fits the workbench idea of physical things you made, but it's the most decorated of these.

**11. Rubber stamps for project types.** Each type (music video, organization, book…) gets a small, slightly tilted stamp in your handwriting, like a mark stamped on paper. The list stays the same; the stamps add the handmade touch. A row of all the stamps at the top could also filter the list.

**12. Ticket stubs.** Each project as a small ticket with a perforated edge. The main part has the title and description, and the torn-off stub holds the year and role. Tactile, playful, and readable on any screen.

My pick is **8, the wall of names**. It's the boldest while staying the leanest, it matches your serif titles, it needs no images, and it says "I make all kinds of things" faster than any list. **9** is the runner-up if you want something more physical.

*You Love My Arrogance.* Part of *Maturity is a Scam*, an album by Vishay Khxl.

I wrote the full narrative and directed the video. Vishay Khxl plays two versions of himself — the video opens with one of them getting punched and falling to the floor. You don't know who did it yet.

## Story

The alter ego has a bandana. He does the full Ashton Hall morning routine — cold water, washing teeth — and caps it off with 30 minutes staring at himself in the mirror wearing fake iron teeth. Played completely straight.

<https://ik.imagekit.io/johnchque/website/projects/ylma/ylma_1.mp4>

The two of them end up at the same party. I shot a beer pong scene where they appear to play against each other using camera blocking and cuts, no split screen. The alter ego loses, sweeps the cups off the table.

Three sessions over three weeks in Copenhagen on a Sony A7 III with a 28-70mm kit lens, shooting in raw. Supporting cast of extras. No crew, no formal training — I figured it out as we went.

For the beer pong and fight scenes we recorded each side separately — first one Vishay, then the other, with different clothing — and cut between them with fast edits to sell the illusion. No special effects. Edited in Kdenlive.

The code is right, but your running dev server is still using the old versions of the two plugins that build videos and images.

**What I found:**
- **Your dev server** on `localhost:4321` serves the YLMA page with only two media blocks, both normal width. The two `.mp4` clips don't appear as videos at all, and `#wide` shows up inside an image link.
- **A fresh build** has all four media blocks wide, the clips play as videos, and no `#wide` appears in any link.

**Why:** `astro.config.mjs` loads these plugins once, when the dev server starts. Editing them doesn't reload them. So your server is running the old plugins, which don't know about `#wide`. Your Markdown changed, so the page re-rendered, but with the old code. That's why the clips disappeared: the old plugin doesn't recognise an `.mp4` link ending in `#wide`.

**Fix:** stop the dev server and start it again:

```
npx astro dev --force
```

That loads the new plugins and clears the cached Markdown. Any future change to the plugins will need a restart too, but content and component changes reload on their own.

OK, what should a good project description have? I feel that YLMA is fine but not the best

A good project page answers, roughly in this order:

1. **What is it, in one breath?** The description line at the top already does this.
2. **Why did it exist?** Who asked, what the song or cause was about, what you wanted to say.
3. **What was the idea?** The concept or central choice that makes this project different from a generic version of it.
4. **What did you actually do?** Your hands on it, concretely. This is what a Danish employer or collaborator reads for.
5. **How did you make it work?** Constraints, decisions and tricks. This shows craft.
6. **What happened after?** Release, reactions, numbers if you have them, or simply how it landed.
7. **What did it teach you?** One or two honest sentences. This is your reflective voice, and it's what makes it *your* page rather than a press release.
8. **Credits.** The people.

**How YLMA does against that:**

- **Strong:** 3, 4 and 5. The bandana, the Ashton Hall routine, the beer pong done with blocking and cuts, no crew, a kit lens, Kdenlive. These details make it believable and fun to read.
- **Missing: why.** How did it come about? What is the song about, and what did Vishay want? Right now it starts with the title repeated, then jumps straight to "I wrote the narrative."
- **Missing: the meaning.** The video is a satire of macho-influencer masculinity, and that's the most interesting thing about it. It also connects to your pro-feminist work (HQNV, Difficult Hugs), which is a thread through your whole workbench. The page never says it out loud.
- **Missing: after and learned.** There's nothing about the release, the reception, or what you'd do differently. The closing "People can sit with that" is nice but sits mid-story.
- **Credits mixes people and gear.** Camera, lens, format and editor aren't credits. They'd read better as a short line in Production, or as rows in the facts at the top. Credits would then be just the people: Vishay, you, the extras.
- **Small things:** the opening line "*You Love My Arrogance.* Part of *Maturity is a Scam*…" repeats the title. It could become "The second single from Vishay Khxl's album *Maturity is a Scam*…" or similar. And a few em dashes could be simpler punctuation if you want it plainer.

If you answer these, I can help shape the missing parts in your voice:

1. How did the project start? Did Vishay come to you with the song, or was it your idea?
2. What did you want people to feel or think about the macho-influencer character?
3. How did it land after release: views, comments, anything someone said to you?
4. What's one thing it taught you, or that you'd do differently?

---
title: "Raaz"
date: 2025-10-10

I directed, filmed and edited it.

## The idea

Raaz means secret. The song is about someone he loved who had to stay hidden from the world, but never from him. Instead of a full story, we went for a simple visualizer that carries the melancholy of the song. Vishay walks around Copenhagen as if he were calling the person he loves, and in some parts he tells her what he is singing.

## Production

I used the same gear as in You Love My Arrogance, a Sony A7 III with the 28-70mm kit lens, and we recorded around the city on two different days.

## After

The song was very well received on Spotify, and the video got a good reception too.

Compared to You Love My Arrogance, this one was less about directing people and more about editing. It taught me a lot about color grading, subtitles, and making the picture follow the music.

## Credits

- **Artist** — Vishay Khxl
- **Director, camera & edit** — John Choque
